strengths: The virtual-correspondence construction is an original, useful approach to a difficult geometric estimation problem. Generating mean-point correspondences allows four-point three-view hypotheses to reuse established 5-point/6-point and P3P solvers. Its simplicity and compatibility with robust estimation are meaningful contributions, despite its explicitly approximate nature.

The calibrated-camera results demonstrate practical gains. In Table 2, 4p3v(M)+R+F achieves PhotoTourism AUC@10 of 69.06 at 30.54 ms, compared with 66.63 at 76.45 ms for the HC baseline. The shifted, refined, filtered variant nearly matches 5pt+P3P accuracy (70.47 versus 70.54) while reducing runtime from 105.50 to 75.78 ms.

The evaluation is substantial: 5,000 triplets per scene across PhotoTourism and Cambridge Landmarks, two RANSAC frameworks, noise experiments, controlled outlier experiments, and scene-specific speed–accuracy curves. Supplementary results using the maximum error across all three camera pairs strengthen the conclusions beyond the main paper's averaged metric.

The main method is training-free and reasonably well explained. Ablations support the shift magnitude and short refinement schedule, with a separate scene used for parameter validation. The authors acknowledge approximation error, scene dependence, and the limited benefit of learning. Overall, the supported calibrated-camera contribution provides a stronger case for acceptance than the limitations provide against it.
weaknesses: The unknown-focal-length extension has a weaker practical case. In Table 3, 4p3vf(M) obtains AUC@10 of 49.88 versus 56.79 for 6pt+P3P, with slightly greater runtime (12.67 versus 11.72 ms). Even the most accurate proposed variant remains less accurate and takes 259.63 ms. Using fewer correspondences remains valuable, but its intended robustness or runtime advantage is not demonstrated here. Focal-length estimation errors and direct accuracy comparisons with existing 4p3vf solvers are also absent.

Reliability of the mean-point approximation remains primarily empirical. The triangle-intersection lemma supplies a potentially loose image-space bound, without controlling pose error or convergence of refinement. The acknowledged degradation under small overlap is consequential, but there is no quantitative breakdown showing how performance changes with overlap, parallax, or depth variation. The evidence supports useful behavior on the tested scenes more strongly than general reliability.

The learned component contributes little demonstrated benefit after refinement while substantially increasing runtime: on PhotoTourism, L+R achieves AUC@10 of 69.88 at 297.88 ms, versus 69.90 at 74.94 ms for M+R. Furthermore, Equation (2) specifies a signed residual as the Sampson loss; minimizing it literally would favor negative residuals rather than zero epipolar error. This may be a notation error, but the actual training objective is ambiguous.

Some reporting and reproducibility details need clarification. Table 9 gives identical accuracy values and nearly identical runtimes for corresponding L±δ and M±δ variants, despite the network overhead reported in Table 10. Numerical RANSAC inlier thresholds and the precise refinement objective are insufficiently specified, and code availability is only promised. These issues limit independent verification, particularly of the learned variants, without establishing a failure of the central mean-based method.
